newsitem.title: INDIA: Dozens of bodies pulled out of blasted India train.
newsitem.headline: Dozens of bodies pulled out of blasted India train.

text.p: Rescuers recovered nearly 60 bodies from a crowded train ripped apart by two bomb blasts in northeastern India, and authorities said on Tuesday they expected to find more victims in the twisted wreckage.
Officials said more victims were expected from the wreckage but not as many as 300 initially believed killed.

Three of the train's 19 coaches-- each crammed with up to 100 people leaving for the New Year holiday-- were destroyed in the blasts after the train left Kokrajhar station in Assam state for Delhi around 7 p.m. (1330 GMT) on Monday, police said.
Rescue workers moved 63 injured to hospitals in two nearby towns and 28 were said to be in a serious condition, a state police spokesman told Reuters by telephone.
There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the attack, which authorities blamed on Bodo tribal guerrillas who have waged a violent separatist struggle for nearly a decade.
A police spokesman in Kokrajhar said none of the estimated 160 passengers in the two sleeper coaches which took the brunt of the explosions were believed to have survived.
"It appeared that there were no survivors in the two coaches," he said.
By afternoon on Tuesday 59 bodies had been recovered at the site of the attack in the town of Sensapani some 200 km (125 miles) west of Guwahati, authorities said.
Dozens of mutilated bodies, some of them children, lay on a soft rice paddy field near the tracks.
Darkness and the remoteness of the region initially hampered rescuers and compounded confusion over the number of dead.
Soon after the explosions, a senior police officer in Assam's biggest city, Guwahati, said at least 300 people were believed dead.

President Shankar Dayal Sharma and Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda condemned the attack. "On behalf of the nation, may I express our sense of shock and condemnation at the terrorist attack," the Press Trust of India quoted Sharma as saying.
Police said a remote-controlled device was used to blow up the Delhi-bound Brahmaputra Mail, an express train named after the sacred river that flows through India's northeast.
Police said copper wire believed to have been attached to the explosives and gelatine sticks were found at the site.

One of the blasts blew a nine-foot (three-metre) deep crater in the ground, witnesses said. A 20-foot (six-metre) section of track was completely destroyed, severing the main rail line between the remote northeast and the rest of India.
The blasts came a day after tribal Bodo guerrillas blew up a road bridge that formed the main road link between the region and the rest of the country, injuring seven people.

A moderate Bodo political leader in Guwahati said the attacks were believed to be tied to a demand by radical Bodo Security Force guerrillas that the central government grant the tribe a separate state by the end of the year.
"This is a message to the central government -- give us a separate state," said the Bodo political leader, who is not linked to separatist groups and asked not to be identified.
More than 1,000 people were travelling on the train, according to officials. Most of the passengers were believed to be holidaymakers heading for Delhi to celebrate the New Year.
The Bodos have demanded a separate tribal state north of the Brahmaputra river since the early 1980s, and their campaign took a violent turn at the end of the decade.
At least 1,000 have died in violence related to the Bodo movement for independence, the United News of India said.
